Armageddon Cave

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The deepest dry cave discovered in South Africa...what scientists are saying is the aftermath of the biggest meteorite to hit SA

Summary:
Not far from Johannesburg, deep below the ground, is a quiet, pitch-dark cave that goes on and on and on..As of yet very few people know about this cave. Explorers say it is the deepest dry cave system in South Africa. In some ways, being there is like under the sea. But its start was anything but peaceful... The cave was probably created in the aftermath of the biggest meteorite ever to hit the earth, the impact that formed the Vredefort dome, 2 billions of years ago.
The first anyone knew of Armageddon cave was when a sinkhole in a mealie field, had its bottom fall out...


Further information:
In the 1990’s, a farmer west of Johannesburg woke up with a start in the early hours of the morning. He heard a tremendous crash. When it was light, one of the farm workers with eyes as wide as saucers ran to him with the news, that there was a sinkhole in the mealie field. And so it was 18m across and 50 m deep.
For the next few years nothing much happened. The sinkhole was dangerous, but convenient for throwing away old tyres and other useless things.
Then some years later... another crash. On one side, the bottom of the sinkhole had disappeared. It just fell through. Now you could see there was something else below the sinkhole… something even deeper than the sinkhole itself.
Some time later, a cave explorer by the name of Colin Redmayne-Smith heard about the sinkhole. Colin is a member of the Speleological Exploration Club, or SEC. They are a bunch of volunteer professionals who find and explore caves in their free time.
Colin showed Steven Tucker and others from SEC the sinkhole on the 13th of Jan 2013. Steven is a qualified chartered accountant, or CA.
"From the top of the sinkhole we could see that, in one corner at the bottom, a shadow hinted at possibilities of darkness beyond. But we weren't too optimistic to find a new cave."
About a week later, on the 19th of Jan 2013, they went back. This time they took ropes and other stuff to descend to the bottom of the sinkhole.
"I went down first, down to the bottom of the sinkhole. I looked into the darkness where the bottom had fallen through and thought... this really could be a new cave there. But then I had to climb up the rope to go back and tell the others."
Steven Tucker: At the bottom I could see blackness stretching away from me. I shouted up to the others that we had something interesting and the next person should start coming down. At this point I also ran out of rope . I slowly slid down a steep slope into that blackness..
I entered a massive chamber, over a 100 meters long and 50 meters wide. My light was lost in there, it was so huge.
I walked along this large chamber and my heart sank as I saw a wall of rocks in front of me. I thought the cave had ended. When the second person, Lindin Mazilis, joined me, we carried on along this wall and found a large passage leading onwards. I had found some small pieces of virgin cave before, but nothing even close to this.
John Dickie is the ropework and rigging specialist at SEC. He's been leading the exploration of the cave with Steven Tucker. It took quite a few trips to set up the ziplines. But they are necessary. What these guys call 'pits' most of us would call 'kloofs' or 'gorges'. The ziplines go over three very deep gorges inside Armageddon. After the third zipline the cave really opens up into an enormous space.
So most of the Armageddon explorers who helped out with all this do caves in their spare time. But then there are people who go down caves to have fun... and do research. Pedeo Boshoff is a geologist who is also a member of SEC, he’s been down the cave.
When he got down into the gigantic cave, he noticed something unusual about the rocks inside. They had been torn apart, much like a paper tissue can be torn apart.
The rocks were sloping in a very unique way. I’d never seen anything like this before. The rock structures had been mangled by tremendous forces. Forces so huge and so sudden that none of the usual suspects could be held liable. It was clear that something had to be behind the rock structures, something that could create tear rocks apart...
Pedro decided to combine his hobby and his profession. He would research how the cave was formed for his Masters thesis in Geology at the University of Johannesburg. So he introduced his study supervisors, Prof Jan Kramers and Dr Herman van Niekerk, to Armageddon. On the next expedition, Herman joined Pedro and the SEC crew. What the came to realise was probably the only thing that could explain the weirdness of this cave was a meteorite impact.
Pedro Boshoff: “We started to realize that the geological structures we saw in the cave, indicates geological events that could only have happened during the impact of the Vredefort meteorite. The cave is in the area that would have been influenced by the Vredefort impact.
They believe that when the meteorite struck the ground about 2 billion years ago rocks over a huge area were compressed by the impact. What also happened is that some rock layers sort of 'slipped' across each other. Where the rocks are 'torn', we're seeing low angle thrust faults. Soon after that the rock expanded again, and deep vertical tears were formed in the structures. These structures allowed cave formation to begin. It is a process that is still continuing today.”
Herman van Niekerk: After the impact events formed the initial cave cavity, the water level within the dolomites filled it. Then the water started to dissolve the surrounding dolomite rocks, which enlarged the initial fractures. Later when the water table dropped, speleothems such as stalagmites and other dripstone formations started to grow. The speleothems create the impression that the cave is a ‘normal’ solution cavity, but it isn't.
They are hopeing to find a certain mineral called sericite, this mineral acts like a geological clock.
Herman :Once we find some sericite, we will know exactly how old the cave is.
Visually this story already has amazing pics and video of the cave and stalacites, rock formations, weird sparkly things. They also have the first climb down, setting up the wires, and the first discoveries but it still important we go down which will take at the very least a day and some go pros and cameras which are protected from the very fine dust that clings to everything. Because all the cave explorers do this in their spare time and logistically for safety reasons (our safety!) and because expert help is required. we need the whole team so we have provisionally set down the 18th April.
Even more visual and high tech is Steve Tucker has been mapping cave so far he’s done 3.7kms.
The roof is so high, the only way we can measure it is with these laser pointers. We keep finding more extensions and more levels... we know the Armageddon system has at least three levels, and is at least 350meters deep. And we keep finding more fascinating things... a waterfall you can hear but can’t see, deep mud pits, and so on.
Other interesting stuff :
The cave is yellow and red and about 20m high.
There is pure black stalagmite on cave floor.
There is a stalacite that fell to floor, shining a torch on it it becomes blue or green because, the geologist says it contains cobalt.
There is a lot of sparkly white stuff ( aragonite) growing on rocks

Press Release:


Armageddon Cave
About an hour west of Johannesburg, deep below the ground, is a cave that has yet to reveal secrets of its astounding limits to the carefully chosen group of explorers and scientists who have descended into its infinite darkness. Carte Blanche cameras descend into a cavern so awesome in size and character that it’s aptly been named Armageddon.


Script:


V/O 4 and a half sec

In an undisclosed area about 45 minutes south west of Johannesburg……….

Link
In the 1990’s, a farmer woke up in the early hours of the morning to a tremendous crash. When light broke, a farm worker came running toward him shouting “There is a sinkhole in the mealie field!” And so there was – about 18m across and 50m deep. That's about as deep as a 12-storey office block is high.

Link
The farmer got nervous and moved his house to another part of his farm. For the next few years nothing much happened. They used the hole for throwing away old tyres and other waste.

Link
Then a few years later... another crash. On one side, the bottom of the sinkhole had disappeared. And it was very clear from that point there was something beyond something a lot deeper.

V/O 21 sec
Rumours of this mysterious sinkhole enticed Gauteng’s Speleological Exploration Club- which consists of a bunch of caving enthusiasts who explore caves in their free time…
And so one Saturday in January 2013, a group of these explorers set out to explore this enormous sinkhole. The first one down was Gerrie Pretorius.

Gerrie Pretorius
Speleological Exploration Club

Gerrie: I was the first, its not something anyone wants to do at first I voluntered no one else was feeling up tp it.
V/O 4 sec
But Gerrie’s rope was just 5 metres to short

Gerrie: I was almost down and I saw this vast blackness just disappearing in there but had to turn back and go up again. I could have been the first guy at the bottom of this new world.

V/O 4 and a half sec
So Steven Tucker went down with a longer rope. He reached the bottom.

Steven Tucker
Speleological Exploration Club

Steven Tucker: You just see this black space in front of you and as a caver that’s really exciting because that means that theres a big passage there and walking through the chamber suddenly a wall in front of me and I actually thought that the cave had ended and my heart dropped for a moment but after a bit more searching a massive passage carried on.
John: Was it scary?
Steven: You don’t know what going to happen, so it’s a bit of the unknown you have to get over.
Pedro : Steven told me about this cave and I came out here and stopped over there got my kit out nonchalantly walked this side of the cave and stuck my head over the edge of this thing and I literally went like this…Oh Shit

Pedro Boshoff
Masters Student, Dept. of Geology
University of johannesburg

V/O 8 sec
Pedro Boshoff , a masters geology student at the University of Johannesburg is passionate about exploring the unknown worlds of caves.

Pedro: What you see is a hole and then it goes down and bowls out way way down there you can see the bottom only just ..this is a very different kettle of fish

V/O 6 sec
This cave is the deepest dry cave ever to have been discovered in South Africa.

John: Did you ever imagine it would be as big as it was?
Steven: I don’t think anyone had a clue that it was that big and then it turned into one of SA’s biggest caves. just knowing I was one of the first people down there that’s very special.
John: once you are down there what did you find?
Pedro: Well after my heart beat normalised, I took my kit off I literally walked to the wall and stuck my hand out, touched the side of the wall and the whole wall was cataclasmic now cataclasmic is rock that has been shattered by only one thing shock immedietely realised something very different going on here…
V/O 7 secs
If Pedro was right not only did this look like evidence of a meteor strike but one of the clearest examples.

LINK
The cave was probably formed in the aftermath of the biggest meteor strikes to ever hit the earth, that was when the Vredefort dome was formed about, 2 billions of years ago.

V/O 25 sec
The Vredefort Dome in the Free State is the result of a meteorite that hit the earth 2 billion years ago, It is the oldest know meteorite impact ever found on earth.

Pedro defided to research the formation of the cave for his Masters thesis in Geology.. On the next expedition, Herman van Niekerk Pedro’s study supervisor joined Pedro.

Dr Herman van Niekerk
Senior Lecturer, Dept. of Geology
University of johannesburg

Herman I was just shocked at the size and the depth of the sinkhole and then seeing how large the chambers are.
John: Are you convinced it was formed by a meteor strike?
Herman: Well we are very close to being a 100% confirmed but based on all the structures and things we have seen it is very very likely that this cave formed as a result of structures that was formed during the Vredefort Meteorite impact.

V/O 8 sec
The University of Johannesburg gave Carte Blanche an exclusive preview of this super cave,as long as we kept the location a secret.

John:. Obviously at the moment its important its kept a secret why is that?
Steven: Specifically for the danger of it, we have very specific ways we rig the caves to avoid these loose rocks and someone who hasn’t been here before might not know how to do that.

V/O 10 sec
Exploring a cave of this size cannot happen without John Dickie, he’s the ropework and rigging specialist of the club,…it is simply too dangerous.

John Dickie
Speleological Exploration Club

John: Here we are nervous times how did the rigging go
John: Went well, distracting having you guys here…

V/O 23 and a half sec
John has devised an innovative technique using his Land Rover diff lock to winch up the cavers when they are done exploring. In this trip down we’ve packed extra strong lights to fim the massive cave chambers. The dolomite in the cave drinks in the light so this will be the first time the enormous spaces are seen clearly. This cave has been christened Armageddon.

John Is Armageddon a good name?
John: Yes down the bottom it looks like a battle has taken place shattered rock, there is another big cave in the country called Apocolypse, when you are standing at the bottom you think how am I going to get out of here

V/O 13 sec
With that comforting thought we set off to discover the world of Armegeddon. Using a single line technique and a hand-held friction device which controls the speed of descent, the cavers lower themselves down.

Link
I’ve now come down 60 metre into sinkhole its astonishing to think cave only really starts here lets see what cave has in store for us…

V/O 13 sec
A further 50 metres down a steep slope, and we’re in a massive chamber. Then the 100 metre or so walk begins. The terrian is rocky, loose stones everywhere and huge boulders we climb over.

Steven: It’s a very diff cave to what we usually have. Usually our caves are very maze like. This is essentially one massive passage heading in one direction and also goes very deep much deeper than we have ever found so far in SA.
Link
We are about 125 m beneath the surface now and its inevitable that you start finding weird and wonderful formations and this is an example of that it’s a stalamite that contains high lebvels of cobalta and copper the climbers have dubbed it Frodo’s sword

V/O 3 sec
In some areas, Araganite crystels line the cave walls

John: It’ from another world isnt it?
Steven: It is.

V/O 8 and a half sec
And it’s here were Pedro noticed something unusual about the rocks, they looked torn apart, something had to be behind these unique rock structures
Herman: When Pedro told me about this I came to have a look when I stood here the first time and saw this no doubt in my eyes there is something huge happening here to break this amt of rock you need a hell of an impact
John: So why are these formations so nb in proving a meteorite strike?
Herman: Because we are seeing compression obviously if you hit something with a big impact you are having a huge compression and what happens is rocks will get pushed over each other, then very soon after that happens we had relaxation and it forms fracture zones which is very perpendicular to the direction of movement and when this opened up we then started forming the deeper parts of the cave..along these fracture zones.

V/O 12 sec
After the impact, the cave filled up with water. Water which started to dissolve the dolomite rocks and enlarge the fractures so creating this cave. Dripstone formations started to grow.

Pedro: These bulbous structures also Know as Cave Popcorn, in fact you can see mud left behind in freaquatic environment. This mud clearly indicating at some point in freaquatic environ ment
John In other words underwater?
Pedro: Underwater.

V/O 7 sec
To get to the last chamber to date. You need to cross three gorges or pits as the team call them.

Steven: In the cave we have these 3 very deep pits that are very dangerous, walls of them are crumbly, normally in a cave you would go down the one side and go up the other side but heres the risk of rock falls a you go down and up, so we have decided to take out the risk and just go straight across the pits.
V/O 8 sec
It took a few challenging trips to set these zip lines up, The first two are made of rope the last is made of steel

Pedro: First one is not a problem you have just got to run on side of the pit and you hook up with your safety line..walk on a little ledge like this but the next two is a zip line over these two pits and the only way to do it is to hook up and you just let go ..because gravity feeds you over this pit almost half way so you go half way and stop and come back…. Now you have to grab rope and power yourself across.

Link
Well I’ve just crossed the second pits on a zip line the third and longest zipline is about 50 metres in that direction we are told it traverses a pit about 150

V/O 10 sec
Steven ‘s been down Armageddon 25 times, they have mapped 4 000 metres of passages, mapping it because they convinced there is much more to it…already there are 4 000 metres of mapped passages.

Steven: theres still some possibilities to push it further and that’s what we are working on most of the time. It’s long days 12/15 hr trips to get to the back there, starting to look at sleeping over there at the back to properly push it.
Link
This is the infamous third pit at this stage we are about 220 metres below the surface – at one time that was a caving record in SA on the other side of that zip line lies a massive cavern, sadly because of the scale of the drop here this is the end of the road for the CB team.

Steven: You cross that 3rd zipline and then suddenly there is a chamber that is 30m wide and lamost 100 metres long, the roof is like 40 metres above your head its like you cant even compare it to a cathedral a cathedral is small.
V/O 13 sec
The exploration of Armagesson has only just begun, with every new reveal, new questins are asked, how much more of it is there, how deep are the pits., for the geologists the fun has only just begun.

Herman: Everytime we go there its like a child in a sweet shop we ..part of the problem is the size of it make difficult to see things you cant stand on one side of the chamber and see something you have to go there.
Pedro: What makes it so special that this is probably in the world the best demonstration example of impact what we term impact induces speregenosis, clearly also the oldest. I think that’s rather unique

Link
Well that is by far the most extraordinary thing I have ever done in my life extraordinary and absolutely terrifying,no wonder they call it Armageddon

Carte Blanche cameras descend into a cavern so awesome in size and character that it’s aptly been named Armageddon. Script: V/O 4 and a half sec In an undisclosed area about 45 minutes south west of Johannesburg………. Link In the 1990’s, a farmer woke up in the early hours of the morning to a tremendous crash. When light broke, a farm worker came running toward him shouting “There is a sinkhole in the mealie field!” And so there was – about 18m across and 50m deep. That's about as deep as a 12-storey office block is high. Link The farmer got nervous and moved his house to another part of his farm. For the next few years nothing much happened. They used the hole for throwing away old tyres and other waste. Link Then a few years later... another crash. On one side, the bottom of the sinkhole had disappeared. And it was very clear from that point there was something beyond something a lot deeper. V/O 21 sec Rumours of this mysterious sinkhole enticed Gauteng’s Speleological Exploration Club- which consists of a bunch of caving enthusiasts who explore caves in their free time… And so one Saturday in January 2013, a group of these explorers set out to explore this enormous sinkhole. The first one down was Gerrie Pretorius. Gerrie Pretorius Speleological Exploration Club Gerrie: I was the first, its not something anyone wants to do at first I voluntered no one else was feeling up tp it. V/O 4 sec But Gerrie’s rope was just 5 metres to short Gerrie: I was almost down and I saw this vast blackness just disappearing in there but had to turn back and go up again. I could have been the first guy at the bottom of this new world. V/O 4 and a half sec So Steven Tucker went down with a longer rope. He reached the bottom. Steven Tucker Speleological Exploration Club Steven Tucker: You just see this black space in front of you and as a caver that’s really exciting because that means that theres a big passage there and walking through the chamber suddenly a wall in front of me and I actually thought that the cave had ended and my heart dropped for a moment but after a bit more searching a massive passage carried on. John: Was it scary? Steven: You don’t know what going to happen, so it’s a bit of the unknown you have to get over. Pedro : Steven told me about this cave and I came out here and stopped over there got my kit out nonchalantly walked this side of the cave and stuck my head over the edge of this thing and I literally went like this…Oh Shit Pedro Boshoff Masters Student, Dept. of Geology University of johannesburg V/O 8 sec Pedro Boshoff , a masters geology student at the University of Johannesburg is passionate about exploring the unknown worlds of caves. Pedro: What you see is a hole and then it goes down and bowls out way way down there you can see the bottom only just ..this is a very different kettle of fish V/O 6 sec This cave is the deepest dry cave ever to have been discovered in South Africa. John: Did you ever imagine it would be as big as it was? Steven: I don’t think anyone had a clue that it was that big and then it turned into one of SA’s biggest caves. just knowing I was one of the first people down there that’s very special. John: once you are down there what did you find? Pedro: Well after my heart beat normalised, I took my kit off I literally walked to the wall and stuck my hand out, touched the side of the wall and the whole wall was cataclasmic now cataclasmic is rock that has been shattered by only one thing shock immedietely realised something very different going on here… V/O 7 secs If Pedro was right not only did this look like evidence of a meteor strike but one of the clearest examples. LINK The cave was probably formed in the aftermath of the biggest meteor strikes to ever hit the earth, that was when the Vredefort dome was formed about, 2 billions of years ago. V/O 25 sec The Vredefort Dome in the Free State is the result of a meteorite that hit the earth 2 billion years ago, It is the oldest know meteorite impact ever found on earth. Pedro defided to research the formation of the cave for his Masters thesis in Geology.. On the next expedition, Herman van Niekerk Pedro’s study supervisor joined Pedro. Dr Herman van Niekerk Senior Lecturer, Dept. of Geology University of johannesburg Herman I was just shocked at the size and the depth of the sinkhole and then seeing how large the chambers are. John: Are you convinced it was formed by a meteor strike? Herman: Well we are very close to being a 100% confirmed but based on all the structures and things we have seen it is very very likely that this cave formed as a result of structures that was formed during the Vredefort Meteorite impact. V/O 8 sec The University of Johannesburg gave Carte Blanche an exclusive preview of this super cave,as long as we kept the location a secret. John:. Obviously at the moment its important its kept a secret why is that? Steven: Specifically for the danger of it, we have very specific ways we rig the caves to avoid these loose rocks and someone who hasn’t been here before might not know how to do that. V/O 10 sec Exploring a cave of this size cannot happen without John Dickie, he’s the ropework and rigging specialist of the club,…it is simply too dangerous. John Dickie Speleological Exploration Club John: Here we are nervous times how did the rigging go John: Went well, distracting having you guys here… V/O 23 and a half sec John has devised an innovative technique using his Land Rover diff lock to winch up the cavers when they are done exploring. In this trip down we’ve packed extra strong lights to fim the massive cave chambers. The dolomite in the cave drinks in the light so this will be the first time the enormous spaces are seen clearly. This cave has been christened Armageddon. John Is Armageddon a good name? John: Yes down the bottom it looks like a battle has taken place shattered rock, there is another big cave in the country called Apocolypse, when you are standing at the bottom you think how am I going to get out of here V/O 13 sec With that comforting thought we set off to discover the world of Armegeddon. Using a single line technique and a hand-held friction device which controls the speed of descent, the cavers lower themselves down. Link I’ve now come down 60 metre into sinkhole its astonishing to think cave only really starts here lets see what cave has in store for us… V/O 13 sec A further 50 metres down a steep slope, and we’re in a massive chamber. Then the 100 metre or so walk begins. The terrian is rocky, loose stones everywhere and huge boulders we climb over. Steven: It’s a very diff cave to what we usually have. Usually our caves are very maze like. This is essentially one massive passage heading in one direction and also goes very deep much deeper than we have ever found so far in SA. Link We are about 125 m beneath the surface now and its inevitable that you start finding weird and wonderful formations and this is an example of that it’s a stalamite that contains high lebvels of cobalta and copper the climbers have dubbed it Frodo’s sword V/O 3 sec In some areas, Araganite crystels line the cave walls John: It’ from another world isnt it? Steven: It is. V/O 8 and a half sec And it’s here were Pedro noticed something unusual about the rocks, they looked torn apart, something had to be behind these unique rock structures Herman: When Pedro told me about this I came to have a look when I stood here the first time and saw this no doubt in my eyes there is something huge happening here to break this amt of rock you need a hell of an impact John: So why are these formations so nb in proving a meteorite strike? Herman: Because we are seeing compression obviously if you hit something with a big impact you are having a huge compression and what happens is rocks will get pushed over each other, then very soon after that happens we had relaxation and it forms fracture zones which is very perpendicular to the direction of movement and when this opened up we then started forming the deeper parts of the cave..along these fracture zones. V/O 12 sec After the impact, the cave filled up with water. Water which started to dissolve the dolomite rocks and enlarge the fractures so creating this cave. Dripstone formations started to grow. Pedro: These bulbous structures also Know as Cave Popcorn, in fact you can see mud left behind in freaquatic environment. This mud clearly indicating at some point in freaquatic environ ment John In other words underwater? Pedro: Underwater. V/O 7 sec To get to the last chamber to date. You need to cross three gorges or pits as the team call them. Steven: In the cave we have these 3 very deep pits that are very dangerous, walls of them are crumbly, normally in a cave you would go down the one side and go up the other side but heres the risk of rock falls a you go down and up, so we have decided to take out the risk and just go straight across the pits. V/O 8 sec It took a few challenging trips to set these zip lines up, The first two are made of rope the last is made of steel Pedro: First one is not a problem you have just got to run on side of the pit and you hook up with your safety line..walk on a little ledge like this but the next two is a zip line over these two pits and the only way to do it is to hook up and you just let go ..because gravity feeds you over this pit almost half way so you go half way and stop and come back…. Now you have to grab rope and power yourself across. Link Well I’ve just crossed the second pits on a zip line the third and longest zipline is about 50 metres in that direction we are told it traverses a pit about 150 V/O 10 sec Steven ‘s been down Armageddon 25 times, they have mapped 4 000 metres of passages, mapping it because they convinced there is much more to it…already there are 4 000 metres of mapped passages. Steven: theres still some possibilities to push it further and that’s what we are working on most of the time. It’s long days 12/15 hr trips to get to the back there, starting to look at sleeping over there at the back to properly push it. Link This is the infamous third pit at this stage we are about 220 metres below the surface – at one time that was a caving record in SA on the other side of that zip line lies a massive cavern, sadly because of the scale of the drop here this is the end of the road for the CB team. Steven: You cross that 3rd zipline and then suddenly there is a chamber that is 30m wide and lamost 100 metres long, the roof is like 40 metres above your head its like you cant even compare it to a cathedral a cathedral is small. V/O 13 sec The exploration of Armagesson has only just begun, with every new reveal, new questins are asked, how much more of it is there, how deep are the pits., for the geologists the fun has only just begun. Herman: Everytime we go there its like a child in a sweet shop we ..part of the problem is the size of it make difficult to see things you cant stand on one side of the chamber and see something you have to go there. Pedro: What makes it so special that this is probably in the world the best demonstration example of impact what we term impact induces speregenosis, clearly also the oldest. I think that’s rather unique Link Well that is by far the most extraordinary thing I have ever done in my life extraordinary and absolutely terrifying,no wonder they call it Armageddon

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The deepest dry cave discovered in South Africa...what scientists are saying is the aftermath of the biggest meteorite to hit SA
metadata.Summary: Not far from Johannesburg, deep below the ground, is a quiet, pitch-dark cave that goes on and on and on..As of yet very few people know about this cave. Explorers say it is the deepest dry cave system in South Africa. In some ways, being there is like under the sea. But its start was anything but peaceful... The cave was probably created in the aftermath of the biggest meteorite ever to hit the earth, the impact that formed the Vredefort dome, 2 billions of years ago. The first anyone knew of Armageddon cave was when a sinkhole in a mealie field, had its bottom fall out...
metadata.Further information: In the 1990’s, a farmer west of Johannesburg woke up with a start in the early hours of the morning. He heard a tremendous crash. When it was light, one of the farm workers with eyes as wide as saucers ran to him with the news, that there was a sinkhole in the mealie field. And so it was 18m across and 50 m deep. For the next few years nothing much happened. The sinkhole was dangerous, but convenient for throwing away old tyres and other useless things. Then some years later... another crash. On one side, the bottom of the sinkhole had disappeared. It just fell through. Now you could see there was something else below the sinkhole… something even deeper than the sinkhole itself. Some time later, a cave explorer by the name of Colin Redmayne-Smith heard about the sinkhole. Colin is a member of the Speleological Exploration Club, or SEC. They are a bunch of volunteer professionals who find and explore caves in their free time. Colin showed Steven Tucker and others from SEC the sinkhole on the 13th of Jan 2013. Steven is a qualified chartered accountant, or CA. "From the top of the sinkhole we could see that, in one corner at the bottom, a shadow hinted at possibilities of darkness beyond. But we weren't too optimistic to find a new cave." About a week later, on the 19th of Jan 2013, they went back. This time they took ropes and other stuff to descend to the bottom of the sinkhole. "I went down first, down to the bottom of the sinkhole. I looked into the darkness where the bottom had fallen through and thought... this really could be a new cave there. But then I had to climb up the rope to go back and tell the others." Steven Tucker: At the bottom I could see blackness stretching away from me. I shouted up to the others that we had something interesting and the next person should start coming down. At this point I also ran out of rope . I slowly slid down a steep slope into that blackness.. I entered a massive chamber, over a 100 meters long and 50 meters wide. My light was lost in there, it was so huge. I walked along this large chamber and my heart sank as I saw a wall of rocks in front of me. I thought the cave had ended. When the second person, Lindin Mazilis, joined me, we carried on along this wall and found a large passage leading onwards. I had found some small pieces of virgin cave before, but nothing even close to this. John Dickie is the ropework and rigging specialist at SEC. He's been leading the exploration of the cave with Steven Tucker. It took quite a few trips to set up the ziplines. But they are necessary. What these guys call 'pits' most of us would call 'kloofs' or 'gorges'. The ziplines go over three very deep gorges inside Armageddon. After the third zipline the cave really opens up into an enormous space. So most of the Armageddon explorers who helped out with all this do caves in their spare time. But then there are people who go down caves to have fun... and do research. Pedeo Boshoff is a geologist who is also a member of SEC, he’s been down the cave. When he got down into the gigantic cave, he noticed something unusual about the rocks inside. They had been torn apart, much like a paper tissue can be torn apart. The rocks were sloping in a very unique way. I’d never seen anything like this before. The rock structures had been mangled by tremendous forces. Forces so huge and so sudden that none of the usual suspects could be held liable. It was clear that something had to be behind the rock structures, something that could create tear rocks apart... Pedro decided to combine his hobby and his profession. He would research how the cave was formed for his Masters thesis in Geology at the University of Johannesburg. So he introduced his study supervisors, Prof Jan Kramers and Dr Herman van Niekerk, to Armageddon. On the next expedition, Herman joined Pedro and the SEC crew. What the came to realise was probably the only thing that could explain the weirdness of this cave was a meteorite impact. Pedro Boshoff: “We started to realize that the geological structures we saw in the cave, indicates geological events that could only have happened during the impact of the Vredefort meteorite. The cave is in the area that would have been influenced by the Vredefort impact. They believe that when the meteorite struck the ground about 2 billion years ago rocks over a huge area were compressed by the impact. What also happened is that some rock layers sort of 'slipped' across each other. Where the rocks are 'torn', we're seeing low angle thrust faults. Soon after that the rock expanded again, and deep vertical tears were formed in the structures. These structures allowed cave formation to begin. It is a process that is still continuing today.” Herman van Niekerk: After the impact events formed the initial cave cavity, the water level within the dolomites filled it. Then the water started to dissolve the surrounding dolomite rocks, which enlarged the initial fractures. Later when the water table dropped, speleothems such as stalagmites and other dripstone formations started to grow. The speleothems create the impression that the cave is a ‘normal’ solution cavity, but it isn't. They are hopeing to find a certain mineral called sericite, this mineral acts like a geological clock. Herman :Once we find some sericite, we will know exactly how old the cave is. Visually this story already has amazing pics and video of the cave and stalacites, rock formations, weird sparkly things. They also have the first climb down, setting up the wires, and the first discoveries but it still important we go down which will take at the very least a day and some go pros and cameras which are protected from the very fine dust that clings to everything. Because all the cave explorers do this in their spare time and logistically for safety reasons (our safety!) and because expert help is required. we need the whole team so we have provisionally set down the 18th April. Even more visual and high tech is Steve Tucker has been mapping cave so far he’s done 3.7kms. The roof is so high, the only way we can measure it is with these laser pointers. We keep finding more extensions and more levels... we know the Armageddon system has at least three levels, and is at least 350meters deep. And we keep finding more fascinating things... a waterfall you can hear but can’t see, deep mud pits, and so on. Other interesting stuff : The cave is yellow and red and about 20m high. There is pure black stalagmite on cave floor. There is a stalacite that fell to floor, shining a torch on it it becomes blue or green because, the geologist says it contains cobalt. There is a lot of sparkly white stuff ( aragonite) growing on rocks
